title: Splitting cost and credit for a shared service
subtitle: When one system serves several teams, who pays and who gets the credit
whyItMatters: Every company past a certain size has shared services, and how their cost is split drives team behaviour more strongly than any written guideline.
openingQuestion: A shared queue costs $10,000 a month and four teams use it. How do you split it?
openingOptions: By measured usage, even though measuring costs more effort
By the size of each team, since a bigger team usually generates more load on the system
Do not split it - leave the cost with the team running the queue, since they chose the architecture
explanation: Splitting evenly means the light user subsidises the heavy one, and nobody has any reason to use less. Leaving it with the operating team is worse still: the cost becomes invisible to exactly the people creating it. Splitting by usage costs effort to measure, and it is the only way the number on the invoice connects to the behaviour that produced it.

diagram.label: Split the cost by what was measured
Each team sees its own number

realWorldExample.description: A shared logging platform tripled in cost over a year. The cost sat with the platform team, so none of the four product teams ever saw it. When it was finally split by actual log volume, one team found it accounted for sixty percent of the whole bill because of a single log line inside a loop, added eighteen months earlier for debugging. They deleted it in an afternoon.

sections.text: A shared service raises two questions that cannot be separated: who pays for it, and who gets the credit when it runs well. Getting either one wrong leads to the same place, which is that nobody looks after it.
Three ways to split, three different behaviours

items: Split evenly: cheap to do, and it teaches every team that using more costs nothing more
Split by team size: looks fair, but team size does not correlate with usage
Split by measurement: costs effort to build, and it is the only one connecting the number to behaviour

sections.text: The important part is that all three split the same total correctly. What differs is what they teach the teams, and what gets taught outlasts that month's number by a long way.

The team running a shared service does work whose success, seen from outside, is that nothing happens. When everything runs well the credit goes to the product teams shipping quickly; when there is an incident, the platform team's name is the one that appears. That asymmetry is real and it is why good people leave those teams.

sections.label: Measure what got carried, not only what broke
sections.text: The cheapest fix for that asymmetry is to report both directions with equal prominence. If the dashboard only shows incident counts then the platform team only exists on bad days. Add a line for the work they carried for everyone else - releases run through them, hours saved for other teams - and the picture comes back into balance.

left.label: Cost visible to whoever creates it
left.text: Every team sees its own share each month. Behaviour changes with nobody having to go and ask, because the number speaks.

right.label: Cost pooled in one place
right.text: The platform team gets asked why it costs so much, while being the one party that did not create most of it.

lines: What the split teaches the teams outlasts that month's number.
Success for a shared service, seen from outside, is that nothing happens.

quiz.question: What does splitting a shared cost evenly teach the teams?
options: That using more costs nothing more
That cost is the platform team's problem
That every team is treated as having an equal role in the use of shared infrastructure
That infrastructure cost is a fixed line item and does not need watching month to month
quiz.explanation: The money is split correctly in total, so nothing looks wrong on the books. What is wrong is the signal: when your share does not move with your usage, no team has a reason to use less, and the total climbs steadily.

quiz.question: Why is splitting by team size unreliable?
options: Because team size does not correlate with usage
Because team size changes every quarter
Because large teams own many small services, so it is hard to attribute shared infrastructure
Because it gives teams an incentive to stay small instead of hiring when they need to
quiz.explanation: A three-person team running batch processing can use ten times what a twenty-person interface team uses. Splitting by an unrelated quantity is exactly as invisible to behaviour as splitting evenly.

quiz.question: One team accounted for 60% of the bill through a log line in a loop for 18 months. Why did nobody notice?
options: Because the cost sat with the platform team, so the team creating it never saw it
Because the log volume grew gradually
Because cost tooling usually shows only totals and does not break them down by source
Because that log line sat in a part of the code that is rarely reread after release
quiz.explanation: The other three all slowed the discovery down. The root cause is that the information never reached anyone who could act on it: the only team that could delete that line in an afternoon was the only team that could not see the invoice.

quiz.question: Why do teams running shared services lose good people?
options: Because their success, seen from outside, is that nothing happens
Because the work is repetitive
Because they must answer requests from many teams, making it hard to focus on longer work
Because they rarely take part in the product decisions the company is actually pursuing
quiz.explanation: The other three are true in many places. The first is true everywhere, because it is inherent to the work: when things run well the credit goes to whoever shipped fast, and the platform team's name only appears on the day something breaks.

quiz.question: What is the cheapest way to rebalance that asymmetry?
options: Report the work carried for others in the same place as the incident count
Rotate platform people into product teams on a cycle
Set a satisfaction target with the other teams and measure it through a regular survey
Credit the platform team on every feature that used their infrastructure to ship
quiz.explanation: The other three take organisational effort and need someone else to agree. The first needs one extra line on a dashboard that already exists, and it fixes the actual cause: the platform team currently only appears in reporting on bad days.

keyTakeaways: All three splits divide the total correctly; they differ in what they teach
Splitting by measurement costs the most effort and is the only one tied to behaviour
A cost invisible to whoever creates it is a cost nobody reduces
Success for a shared service, seen from outside, is that nothing happens

practicePrompt.question: A $10,000 invoice, four teams using it in a 60/20/15/5 ratio. Split evenly, how much is the largest user carried by the others?
options: $2,500 (= the gap between the even share and the smallest team's usage)
$1,500 (= the gap between the two middle teams rather than for the largest)
practicePrompt.explanation: That team uses $6,000 and pays $2,500, so the other three carry $3,500 of it every month. That figure is larger than the two small teams' entire usage combined, and it appears nowhere at all under an even split.

summary.keyIdea: Split by measured usage, and report credit alongside blame
summary.commonMistake: Leaving shared cost with the operating team to keep the books tidy
summary.action: Find one shared cost at your company and ask who actually sees it.

application.title: Two questions for every shared service
application.message: Who sees its cost each month? Does any line on the dashboard describe the work it carries for others?
application.secondary: If the first answer is the operating team and the second is no, that service will get both more expensive and short of people.
